extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, law students, and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for inventor and patentee rights, wrongful acts (slander/libel and infringement), and the legal tests for identity, novelty, and remedies in U.S. patent law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's property not lost by unrestricted disclosure (third view)
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor's property in his invention and his right to an immediate remedy in case of its actual or threatened invasion are not affected by its unrestricted disclosure, unless such disclosure is protracted beyond the lawful period or is accompanied by other acts establishing his intention to abandon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This view treats a universally known invention as retaining legal attributes of a secret invention until time or other circumstances show dedication to the public; it is consistent with the purpose of the statute to relieve proof and commercial difficulties faced by inventors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory grace period (two years) for unrestricted disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress fixed a period (two years) within which it is immaterial whether a disclosure were confidential or unrestricted; during that period the inventor's rights are not affected by disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two-year allowance was intended to let the inventor ascertain commercial importance and patentable merit without losing remedies; the statutory limit prevents permanent relinquishment absent other acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor retains same remedies during disclosure period
rubrics_metrics.description: During the period of unrestricted disclosure the inventor's invention may be treated as within his own control as fully as while he still preserved his secret; for unauthorized employment an action for damages must lie and for threatened infraction an injunction must be obtainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages are computed on same general basis as for patent infringement; equitable relief (injunction) is appropriate for threatened invasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract rights in unpatented invention are unimpaired
rubrics_metrics.description: During the disclosure period the law recognizes the contract rights of the inventor over his invention as unimpaired, and affords him ample and immediate remedies for their violation; he can assign or license it with or without right to obtain a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligations from conveyances are enforceable irrespective of issuance of a patent; owner should be protected against tortious as well as contractual invasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent invention by others is not a violation
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent exercise of inventive skill by a different inventor, even if developing the same idea or means, is not a violation of the original inventor's rights; to be liable the wrong-doer must have appropriated the invention from him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two rival inventors may each hold property in their respective inventions; priority disputes are settled upon issuance of a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong against patentee requires damnum and injuria
rubrics_metrics.description: No act constitutes a wrong against the patentee unless it embraces both elements of a tort, the damnum and injuria; a lawful act that merely destroys commercial value (damnum alone) is not actionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts must be directed against the monopoly conferred by the patent (attacking the franchise) to constitute an actionable invasion; examples supplied in text distinguish lawful competitive advances from tortious invasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two forms of injury to patent rights: slander/libel and infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights conferred by a patent are subject to two forms of injury: (1) malicious and public injury to the reputation of the patented invention (slander/libel), and (2) unauthorized use of the invention (infringement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement (unauthorized use) is the principal wrong; slander/libel, though less frequent, can be materially disastrous and is treated separately with its own remedies and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slander/libel by denying patentability is prima facie wrongful
rubrics_metrics.description: The publication, verbal or in writing, of statements impugning the validity of a patent on the ground of the non-patentability of its subject-matter are prima facie wrongful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The issue of a patent constitutes presumptive evidence of patentability; such statements are actionable only when they cause special damage and may be justified or excused by ordinary defenses applicable to slander/libel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slander/libel by denying title (first inventor) actionable if malicious
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements derogatory to the title of the patentee as the first and true inventor are slanders/libels for which a remedy may be obtained when made by persons having no claim to the invention and when malicious and causing special damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rival inventors who claim the invention must act in good faith (e.g., promptly apply for a patent) or lose the excuse for public attack; moderation in language is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rivals may warn public but must use moderate language and act in good faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Rival inventors, whether patentees or not, may protect their interests and warn the public against infringing their rights by giving notice and denying validity of a rival patent, but such notices must be couched in moderate language and refrain from superfluous adverse commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good faith includes making a speedy patent application if entitled; excess beyond necessary information can be libelous and enjoined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for slander/libel: legal action and limited equitable relief
rubrics_metrics.description: The remedy at law for slander against a patent is an action on the case praying damages according to injury actually sustained; equity may or may not enjoin repetition depending on jurisdiction and facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jurisdictions leave past injury to legal remedy only; federal courts have limited cognizance of such actions except in cases between citizens of different States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of infringement (scope of exclusive rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: The issue of a patent confers upon the patentee the exclusive right to make, use, and vend the patented invention throughout the United States and the Territories during the patent term; infringement consists in the manufacture, use, or sale of the invention protected by the patent within that area and time by any person not duly authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement analysis requires identifying the invention, the nature of the alleged act (when, where, by whom, and with what knowledge/intent), and applying propositions to the classes of inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement only of the invention claimed and described
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention whose manufacture, use, or sale constitutes infringement is the invention covered and protected by the patent; the patent protects only the patentable subject-matter which it specifically claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A device not covered by the patent does not infringe even if it effects the same purpose; elements not described or only partially disclosed in the patent (though indispensable) are not susceptible of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity determined by same tests as novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity of the invention made, used, or sold by the alleged infringer with that described and claimed in the patent is determined by the same tests applied in ascertaining novelty when comparing with prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty and infringement are distinct but related; expert evidence and precedents guide the comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity must be identity in the idea of means (not merely results)
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity sought must reside in the idea of means embodied in each invention; the patent secures the means specified to produce a result, not the result itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same end or result may be produced by other means without infringement; the means specified in the patent must be present in substance in the accused device.

rubrics_metrics.name: The patented idea of means must be completely embraced in the accused invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea covered by the patent must be completely embraced in the idea expressed in the infringement; the accused idea may be more comprehensive but still infringe if it contains the patented idea substantially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patented invention used as an element in a later combination may still be an infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity determined by functions, modes, and effects tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity in ideas of means subsists where the compared inventions perform the same functions by the same modes of operation; if effects are substantially different, or functions essentially distinct, or modes radically unlike, there is no identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversely, identical effects, functions, and modes indicate identity; once identity exists, variations in shape, size, arrangement, or materials are unimportant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of essential patented features leads to infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defendant's device or process requires the use of the patented features (essential elements), there is an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of an essential patented feature within a larger combination or device can constitute infringement; mere formal changes or trivial variations typically do not avoid infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: One valid reissue claim may be infringed despite other invalid claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A single valid claim in a reissue may be infringed though other claims of the reissue are not valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This underscores claim-by-claim analysis: infringement may be found as to any valid claim standing in the patent or reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for infringement: damages and injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: For unauthorized employment an action for damages must lie at law, the damages being computed on the same general basis as for patent infringement; for a threatened infraction an injunction must be obtainable in equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages and equitable relief are applied to protect the monopoly conferred by the patent; courts apply established measures (see cited cases) in computing relief.
